checks.title: Cookie security flags
checks.summary: The session cookie session_id can be read by scripts on the page.
checks.explanation: Without HttpOnly, any script running on the page can read the session cookie. That turns a single cross-site scripting bug anywhere on the site into a full account takeover, because the attacker can copy the session rather than needing the password.
checks.fix: Set HttpOnly on session_id. In most frameworks this is one configuration setting rather than a code change.

evidence.scope: cookies set for an anonymous visitor on the homepage

checks.title: Email spoofing protection
checks.explanation: Anyone can send email that appears to come from your domain. Without DMARC, receiving mail servers have no instruction to reject those messages, so invoice fraud and staff impersonation land in inboxes looking legitimate.
checks.fix: Publish a DMARC record at _dmarc.example-business.com starting at p=none so you can see who is sending as you, then tighten to p=quarantine and finally p=reject once the reports look clean.

checks.title: HTTP security headers
checks.explanation: A Content-Security-Policy tells the browser which scripts it is allowed to run. Without one, a single injected script anywhere on the page runs with full access to what your visitors see and type.
checks.fix: Add a Content-Security-Policy, starting in report-only mode so you can see what it would block before it breaks anything.

checks.title: DNS hygiene
checks.summary: Both nameservers belong to a single provider.
checks.explanation: If that one provider has an outage, your website and email both disappear at the same time and you have no way to redirect them. Zone transfers are correctly refused, and no dangling records were found.
checks.fix: Add a secondary DNS provider. Most registrars support this and it is usually a configuration change rather than a migration.

checks.title: Certificate history
checks.explanation: These logs are public and searchable by anyone, which is what makes them useful to an attacker looking for hostnames you have not advertised. The list here is short enough to review by eye.
checks.fix: No action needed. Certificate transparency is public, so it is worth occasionally checking this list for names you do not recognise.

checks.title: Exposed files
checks.summary: None of the three checked paths are reachable.
checks.explanation: Development files left on a live server can expose source code, database passwords and API keys to anyone who requests them directly. None were found here.

checks.title: TLS configuration
checks.summary: TLS 1.3 with a strong cipher; the certificate has 64 days left.
checks.explanation: Traffic between your visitors and your site is encrypted with a current protocol, and the outdated versions that attackers target are refused.
checks.fix: No action needed. Confirm certificate auto-renewal is running so this does not lapse.
